articles.title: Neuroimmune-Lipid Crosstalk in Chronic Itch: Molecular Mechanisms from Skin Surface to Cerebral Cortex.
articles.abstract: Chronic pruritus is a complex sensory disorder arising from interactions among epidermal barrier dysfunction, immune signaling, peripheral sensory neurons, spinal circuits, and supraspinal networks. Bioactive lipids participate in this neuroimmune crosstalk as both structural components of the skin barrier and signaling mediators. Altered ceramide composition and sphingolipid metabolism accompany barrier dysfunction, while sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P), eicosanoids, and autotaxin-derived lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) modulate inflammatory and sensory pathways. In particular, experimental studies implicate S1P-S1PR3-transient receptor potential (TRP) signaling and LPA receptor pathways in peripheral pruriception, although their causal relevance to human chronic itch remains incompletely established. These mechanisms interact with cytokines including interleukin (IL)-31, thymic stromal lymphopoietin, and IL-33 to enhance sensory-neuron responsiveness. Within the spinal dorsal horn, gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP)/GRPR-dependent circuits integrate pruriceptive input and are modulated by neuroimmune signaling, potentially contributing to central sensitization. Supraspinal sensory, affective, motivational, and reward-related networks may further reinforce the itch-scratch cycle. This review integrates lipid metabolism, neuroimmune signaling, and neural plasticity across peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal levels, with emphasis on atopic dermatitis (AD), prurigo nodularis (PN), psoriasis, and systemic pruritic disorders, and discusses therapeutic strategies and research priorities for mechanism-based treatment of chronic itch.

articles.title: Dynamic stratum corneum ceramide alterations reflect barrier dysfunction and clinical response to topical chlormethine treatment in early-stage mycosis fungoides.
articles.abstract: Early-stage mycosis fungoides (MF), a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, presents as patches and/or plaques with an impaired skin barrier. The stratum corneum (SC) lipid matrix is important for skin barrier function. Alterations in the SC ceramide profile have been linked to a reduced barrier function in benign inflammatory skin diseases and might also be an underlying factor in the impaired barrier function in MF. Therefore, we characterized barrier function and SC ceramide profiles in lesional and non-lesional skin of 21 patients with early-stage MF and 10 healthy controls, and assessed how these barrier and ceramide characteristics evolve during chlormethine gel treatment in patients. Barrier function was measured by transepidermal water loss. SC ceramides were collected by tape stripping and analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Local inflammatory markers were measured in suction blister fluid. At baseline, MF lesions showed impaired barrier function accompanied by distinct changes in the SC ceramide profile, including altered ceramide subclass composition and reduced ceramide chain length. These abnormalities occurred in the context of a predominantly type 1-skewed inflammatory milieu. Importantly, both barrier dysfunction and ceramide alterations were dynamic and improved in patients with a clinical response to chlormethine gel treatment, alongside reduced lesion severity and local inflammation. Longitudinal associations of ceramide characteristics with barrier function, clinical lesion severity, and inflammatory markers support SC ceramide alterations as dynamic correlates of MF disease activity. Together, these findings suggest that SC ceramide alterations may reflect a downstream consequence of inflammation that is shared across inflammatory dermatoses.

articles.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes With Episoft® AC SPF 50+, a Ceramide-Based Moisturizer, in Acne-Related Post-procedural Care: A Real-World Multicenter Observational Study From India (PROCEED Study).
articles.abstract: Post-procedural skin barrier disruption following acne-related dermatological procedures causes significant patient discomfort and heightens ultraviolet (UV) sensitivity. Ceramide-based formulations with broad-spectrum photoprotection can address barrier repair and sun protection factor (SPF) in a single step. However, patient-reported evidence supporting their use in this setting is still limited.

articles.title: Prevention and Management of Pediatric Sensitive Skin Conditions in India: A Modified Delphi Consensus.
articles.abstract: Sensitive skin poses significant dermatological challenges in the pediatric population, necessitating thorough exploration and understanding. In this study, we aim to provide neonatologists, pediatricians, dermatologists, and allergists in India with consensus-based recommendations for the prevention and management of sensitive skin in the pediatric age group. A modified Delphi method was used to arrive at a consensus. A group of 15 experts with experience in pediatric skincare constituted the panel. Panel members representing diverse specialties from the major regions of India participated in the consensus process. Statements were developed based on a structured review of the literature identified through PubMed/Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE) (January 2000 to May 2024; updated in March 2025) using the keywords "sensitive skin," "pediatric," "emollient," "prevention," and other related terms

articles.title: Effect of human skin storage on stratum corneum drug penetration assessed by confocal Raman spectroscopy.
articles.abstract: Fresh human skin is the preferred model for ex vivo dermal penetration studies. However, limited availability often necessitates frozen storage. We investigated whether storage for two months at -20 °C or -80 °C affects skin barrier function, selected Raman-derived skin properties, and drug penetration. For each of six donors, paired full-thickness abdominal skin samples were analyzed fresh or after frozen storage. Barrier integrity was assessed by transepidermal water loss, while quantitative confocal Raman spectroscopy was used to determine water concentration profiles and the amount of caffeine, diclofenac sodium, and salicylic acid within the upper 15 µm after application of 2% (w/w) hydrogels for 1 h. Transepidermal water loss varied across storage conditions, although neither frozen-storage condition differed significantly from fresh skin. Raman-derived water content was significantly higher after storage at -80 °C than in fresh or -20 °C-stored skin, whereas no consistent storage-related differences were detected in the fingerprint spectra or combined ceramide and fatty acid signal. articles.title: Ceramide Metabolic Pathways and Their Regulation in Adolescent Acne Vulgaris.
articles.abstract: Ceramides constitute approximately 50% of the lipid mass in the stratum corneum and are essential for epidermal permeability barrier function. In acne vulgaris, barrier disruption is accompanied by altered ceramide composition, yet the molecular mechanisms that connect acne-associated signals to specific changes in ceramide metabolism remain incompletely understood. This review integrates evidence from lipidomic profiling, enzymatic pathway characterization, and inflammatory signaling studies to examine how ceramide biosynthesis and turnover are modulated in acne-prone skin. articles.title: Effectiveness and Safety of a Moisturizer Containing Centella Asiatica Extract, Ceramide NP, and Panthenol for Erythema and Skin Barrier in Erythematotelangiectatic Rosacea: A Randomized Controlled Trial Study.
articles.abstract: Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea is a chronic recurrent inflammatory disease that often impose a significant psychological burden on patients. Given that effective moisturization is integral to its management, the choice of a proper moisturizer is a critical clinical consideration. Our study aims to assess the effectiveness and safety of a moisturizer containing Centella asiatica extract, ceramide NP, and panthenol for erythema and skin barrier in Chinese patients with erythematotelangiectatic rosacea.

articles.title: Enzymatic Synthesis of a Novel α-Linolenic Acid-Enriched Phytoceramide From Perilla Seed Oil and Its Multifunctional Bioactivity in Skin Barrier Repair and Anti-Aging.
articles.abstract: Ceramides are essential lipid components of the skin barrier, accounting for approximately 50% of intercellular lipids in the stratum corneum. Their deficiency is associated with various skin disorders, including atopic dermatitis and xerosis. This study aimed to enzymatically synthesize a novel phytoceramide from perilla seed oil (PSO-Cer) and evaluate its multifaceted bioactivity, including skin barrier enhancement and anti-aging effects, in comparison with oleic acid-derived Ceramide IIIB. PSO-Cer was synthesized enzymatically and characterized by HPLC-CAD and LC-QTOF. Its biological effects were assessed in human keratinocytes (HaCaT) and dermal fibroblasts-adult (HDF-a) through cytotoxicity assays, qPCR of genes related to barrier function and extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, western blot, and transcriptome sequencing. HPLC-CAD confirmed PSO-Cer was rich in polyunsaturated fatty acid chains, notably α-linolenic acid (34.49%). Both PSO-Cer and Ceramide IIIB were non-cytotoxic up to 25 µg/mL and significantly upregulated genes critical for epidermal barrier function (FLG, IVL, TGM1, CERS3, and ELOVL4) and ECM components (COL1A1, COL3A1, and ELN) in UVB-irradiated fibroblasts. Transcriptome analysis revealed that while both ceramides shared common mechanisms, namely activation of mTOR signaling and sphingolipid metabolism, PSO-Cer exhibited distinct properties, positioning it as a promising multifunctional active for advanced skincare formulations aimed at comprehensive skin health.

articles.title: Structure-function relationship of a single double bond: the difference in lamellar phase behaviors between ceramides NS and NdS.
articles.abstract: The barrier function of mammalian skin is closely related to the unique structure of the complex lipid matrix of the stratum corneum. Within this matrix, the heterogeneous group of ceramides plays a key role in determining barrier properties. As native stratum corneum is highly complex, simplified stratum corneum lipid mixture models can be used to efficiently elucidate their detailed structural arrangement. Here, the application of selected ceramide subspecies with defined chain lengths and head group structures in monomeric lipid mixture models, i.e. containing only a single ceramide subspecies, was found to be meaningful for a step-by-step evaluation of the distinct effects of the individual ceramide. In the present work, non-hydroxylated N-acyl chain ceramides with sphingosine and dihydrosphingosine bases with acyl chain lengths of C18, each fully protiated or partially deuterated, were obtained by chemical syntheses. As sphingosine and dihydrosphingosine-based ceramides differ just in a single double bond at the C4-C5 position of the sphingoid base, the aim of this study was to elucidate the effect of the double bond in the ceramide head groups on the lamellar phase behavior of ceramides incorporated into simplified monomeric stratum corneum lipid model membranes.
